faqs.question: How do I send a Halloween ecard to someone who rarely checks email?
faqs.answer: Send it as a link in the chat app they already use, such as WhatsApp or iMessage, or send a picture card that shows inline. SubhSandesh's Halloween pages are made for this: you publish, copy the private link and paste it into the conversation.

faqs.question: Can I schedule a Halloween ecard to open at a set time?
faqs.answer: On the premium Halloween page, yes: set the optional unlock time and the link shows only their name and a countdown until then. That lets you send it on 29 or 30 October and have it open on the 31st.

faqs.question: Is it rude to send a Halloween ecard on 1 November?
faqs.answer: Not really. In a 2025 study of 754 people, recipients rated a gift two days late at 1.70 for relationship harm on a 1 to 7 scale, while givers guessed 2.29, and a gift never sent scored worse than a late one in a follow-up study.

faqs.question: Does the person need an app to open a Halloween ecard?
faqs.answer: Not for SubhSandesh's Halloween pages: they open in any phone or laptop browser, with no app or account for the recipient. Library ecards also arrive as a link, by email or chat.

faqs.question: How many photos can I put in a Halloween ecard?
faqs.answer: On the regular /happy-halloween page, up to six; on the premium page, up to twelve. A picture card in a chat is one image per card, and library ecards depend on the design.

faqs.question: Are animated Halloween ecards OK for young children?
faqs.answer: Pick one built for them. The kids tone of the regular Halloween page is spooky-cute, with no blood, no gore and no jump scares, nothing goes dark, and it respects reduced-motion settings.

faqs.question: Can I send one Halloween ecard to my whole family group?
faqs.answer: Not with SubhSandesh's Halloween pages, which are one-person greetings. For a group, drop one picture card into the group chat or use a library ecard that sends to a list.

faqs.question: Can I fix a typo after I've sent a Halloween ecard?
faqs.answer: On a SubhSandesh page you can edit and republish at any time, and the same link shows the latest version. A picture card already sent in a chat cannot be changed, so check it before you send.

faqs.question: How will I know if they opened my Halloween ecard?
faqs.answer: On the regular page you get an email the first time they answer the question at the end. On the premium page they can also send one reply of up to 280 characters, which is emailed to you.

faqs.question: How long should a voice note in a Halloween ecard be?
faqs.answer: The premium page takes up to 60 seconds, and shorter is fine. Research on voice versus text found voice builds a stronger bond, so even 20 seconds of you saying their name does work a typed line cannot.

faqs.question: Can I lock a Halloween ecard with a password?
faqs.answer: Yes, both Halloween pages offer an optional password when you publish. Across all SubhSandesh templates, 38.5% of creators set one before sharing (measured 24 September 2026).

faqs.question: What day is Halloween in 2027?
faqs.answer: Sunday 31 October 2027. In 2026 it is Saturday 31 October, and it is 31 October every year.

article.contentMarkdown:
# Halloween Ecards: Which Type to Send and When It Should Land

A Halloween ecard is a greeting that arrives as a link, an email or an image instead of paper, and the right type depends on how much of you the recipient should find inside it. On SubhSandesh, 48.3% of shared pages are opened on a phone (27,725 of 57,456 views), and the average page is viewed 11.1 times, so a card gets reopened rather than glanced at once. Both figures are platform-wide, measured on 24 September 2026; neither is Halloween data.

Below are the four types of Halloween ecards, a table of what each lets you add, what research says about effort, voice and lateness, and send timing for Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027.

## What is a Halloween ecard?

A Halloween ecard is a digital greeting for 31 October that the recipient opens on a screen, usually from a link in an email or a chat. It swaps the envelope for a URL and the printed verse for animation, music, photos or something to tap.

In the ecards people actually send, pictures outweigh words. A 2025 peer-reviewed study in [Neophilology analysed 159 holiday ecards](https://neophilology.elpub.ru/jour/article/view/531), 110 sampled from open-access card sites and 49 that respondents actually sent on 12 June 2023, and found the visual part dominated the verbal part. Those were Russia Day cards, not Halloween ones, but the lesson travels: in a picture-led card the words are the scarce part, so yours carry more weight.

## 4 types of Halloween ecard, and who each one suits

Halloween ecards sort into four broad types. Each entry covers the same four things in order: what it is, who it suits, what the recipient does, and what you put in.

### 1. Membership library ecard

A card picked from a catalogue of professionally animated designs, sent from a service you join. It suits someone sending one polished design to many people, such as grandparents or an office list. The recipient opens an email or link and watches the animation, and you add a name, a typed message and, on designs that allow it, a photo.

### 2. Ad-supported library ecard

The same catalogue model without joining anything. It suits a one-off send to an acquaintance where the gesture matters more than the setting. Where a catalogue runs on advertising, the recipient may see adverts beside your message, so open the card yourself before you send it.

### 3. Picture card sent in a chat

A single image or short clip dropped into WhatsApp, iMessage or Instagram DMs with your own words under it. It suits group chats and people who never tap links, because it shows inline. The recipient scrolls past it like any photo, and once it is sent you cannot change it.

### 4. Interactive Halloween page

A private web page built around one person, holding their name, your photos, your letter and something for them to do. It suits a partner, best friend, sibling or child you are close to. The recipient taps one link that opens in a phone or laptop browser, and on SubhSandesh 90.9% of started pages are published and shared (4,724 of 5,199, platform-wide).

## Halloween ecard types compared: photos, words and replies

The table compares what each type lets you put in and what comes back to you. The two page rows are SubhSandesh's Halloween templates, as their own FAQs describe them in October 2026.

| Ecard type | Words you write | Your photos and voice | What comes back to you |
|---|---|---|---|
| Library ecard (membership or ad-supported) | One message box beside stock artwork | Depends on the design you choose | Whatever reply they send by email or text |
| Picture card in a chat | One caption under the image | 1 image per card; voice only as a separate note | Their reply in the same thread |
| /happy-halloween page | A letter, a word carved on the pumpkin, a question of up to 60 characters | Up to 6 photos, no voice | An email the first time they answer |
| /happy-halloween-premium page | A letter of up to 3,000 characters plus a sealed P.S. | Up to 12 photos and a voice note of up to 60 seconds | One reply of up to 280 characters, emailed to you |

Library cards win on artwork, chat pictures win on reach, and pages win on how much of the two of you fits inside. No single type suits every name on your list.

## Does a Halloween ecard seem less thoughtful than paper?

Probably less than you fear. In a series of preregistered experiments, [Liu and colleagues (2023, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology)](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35816566) found people consistently underestimate how much others appreciate being reached out to, whether by a brief message or a small gift. The underestimate was largest when the message came out of the blue and when the two people were not especially close.

So a Halloween ecard to a distant cousin or an old flatmate is worth more than it feels from your side. The effort a recipient notices is the part no catalogue supplies:

- their name in the first line, not the last
- one memory nobody else was there for
- a photo that exists only on your phone
- a sign-off in the voice you actually use with them

## Voice or text: what to put inside a Halloween ecard

Add your voice if the ecard allows it. In a field experiment and lab chats, [Kumar and Epley (2021, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General)](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/32915017) found that interactions including voice built stronger social bonds than text-only ones, with no rise in awkwardness, yet people expected otherwise and leaned toward text. The study tested conversations, not greeting cards (abstract read), so take it as a strong hint rather than a ruling.

If the card only takes typed words, keep them short and specific. Six original lines for an ecard's message box:

- "Sound on, lights off, then text me which part made you jump."
- "No stock witch could say this properly, so the voice in here is mine, slightly embarrassed."
- "I dug these photos out of the corner of my camera roll. The haunted house was only an excuse."
- "Open it tonight or next week. My ghosts are patient and they have nowhere else to be."
- "Every picture in here is evidence. The letter is my confession."
- "This card cannot carry a pumpkin, so it carries the crooked one we carved together instead."

## When to send a Halloween ecard in 2026 and 2027

Halloween falls on Saturday 31 October 2026 and Sunday 31 October 2027. Aim for the evening of the 30th or the morning of the 31st, before the recipient heads out in costume.

Clocks shift that week. Under [EU Directive 2000/84/EC](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:32000L0084), summer time ends at 01:00 GMT on the last Sunday in October: 25 October in 2026, but Halloween morning itself in 2027, and the UK changes the same day. US clocks change on 1 November 2026 and 7 November 2027, so on both Halloweens London is 4 hours ahead of New York, not 5, and India is 9.5 hours ahead.

Late still beats never. In [Haltman and colleagues' 2025 Journal of Consumer Psychology paper](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/jcpy.1446), 754 participants rated how much a late birthday gift would harm the relationship, on a 1 to 7 scale:

- on time: givers 1.21, recipients 1.39, no real difference
- 2 days late: givers 2.29, recipients 1.70
- 2 weeks late: givers 2.94, recipients 1.73
- never sent (a separate 871-person study): recipients 2.84, against 2.21 for two months late

Those were gifts, not ecards, but a 1 November ecard plainly beats silence. SubhSandesh creators also tend to build close to the day: in the platform's nearest festival measurement, Raksha Bandhan 2026 (n = 89, not Halloween), 49.4% of pages were built on the festival day itself.

## Halloween ecards as a page: the regular or the premium template

If the ecard is for one person you know well, a page gives them something to do rather than something to watch. The [interactive Halloween card with a haunted house and a pumpkin to carve](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween) takes about 5 minutes to make: they knock three times, catch falling sweets, carve the jack-o'-lantern, find your up to 6 photos behind fogged portraits and read your letter by flashlight. You get an email the first time they answer the question at the end.

Choose the [premium Halloween page with a voice note, a reply box and an unlock time](https://subhsandesh.in/happy-halloween-premium) when timing worries you, because you can send it early and the link shows only their name and a countdown until the moment you set. It takes about 10 minutes and holds up to 12 photos, a 60-second voice note and a 3,000-character letter. Both offer an optional password, which 38.5% of SubhSandesh creators set before sharing a page (2,000 of 5,199, platform-wide).

Both have partner, best friend, family and kids modes, and the kids version trades scares for round, blushing ghosts and confetti spiders. For a birthday or another occasion later in the year, [browse every SubhSandesh template](https://subhsandesh.in/templates) instead.

## When another type of Halloween ecard is the better choice

The pages are one-person greetings, so they are the wrong tool for 30 names. For an office list or a family group, a library ecard or one picture card in the group chat takes far less of your time.

Skip the page for anyone who distrusts links or lives inside one messaging app, where a picture card shows inline. The interface is also English only.

The default question is "Will you be my boo?", and on the regular page the No button runs away, so never send that version to someone who has not already said yes. Pick the best-friend or family mode, or rewrite the question. And if the person keeps cards on a shelf, no ecard replaces paper: post one and send the link too.

## Sources

- Savelyeva, T. V., Neophilology 11(3), published 16 October 2025, CC BY 4.0.
- Liu, Rim, Min and Min, Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, online 11 July 2022 (abstract read).
- Kumar and Epley, Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, online 10 September 2020 (abstract read).
- Haltman, Herziger, Donnelly and Reczek, Journal of Consumer Psychology 35(4), online 5 December 2024, CC BY 4.0.
- Directive 2000/84/EC on summer-time arrangements, 19 January 2001.

failed.item: At least one table column uses first-party data
failed.why: Re-checked in the fix pass: facts.md holds no Halloween usage data (BRIEF §3, §9), and the only first-party lines that could fill a column (48.3% phone opens, 11.1 views per page, 38.5% password rate) are platform-wide SubhSandesh figures that say nothing about library ecards or chat pictures, so a column built from them would be blank or misleading for two of four rows. The page rows use first-hand template-spec values, which do not count as first-party data. Closes when a Halloween probe of the gifts DB (pages made, answer emails sent, premium replies per template) can be run after 31 October 2026 and gives a per-type figure such as reply rate for the two page rows.

failed.item: No source passes the **swap test** — none could sit unchanged in a different keyword's post in this batch
failed.why: Re-judged against this batch's 5 posts, not b1–b8 (the writer's reason, reuse in older Halloween batches, is what the cap rules test, not the swap test). Savelyeva 2025 (Neophilology, ecard corpus) and Haltman et al. (late gifts, used here for the 1 November question) fit no sibling. But EU Directive 2000/84/EC is a clock-change source that could sit unchanged in halloween-2027, which already covers the 2026/2027 clock changes via NIST and gov.uk; Liu et al. (reaching out) and Kumar & Epley (voice vs text) are general communication papers, not about cards. Dropping the directive would leave the Halloween-morning clock change unsourced. A replacement ecard-specific source was searched again (Crossref + Europe PMC: 'e-cards versus paper greeting cards perception', 'digital greeting card sender recipient'); hits were paper-card books, an AR-card thesis, and a Routledge (Taylor & Francis, banned) chapter. Closes if an open-access reception study of electronic vs paper greeting cards appears, which could replace Liu, and the clock fact moves to a source only an ecard post would cite (none known).

auditReport.honestAssessment: Hard head term: the measured top 10 is about 3/10 weak and owned by ecard storefronts with large catalogues and long-standing domain authority, so this informational page may not rank for the bare term at all; its realistic win is answer-engine citation for sub-questions (which ecard type, is a 1 November ecard rude, the 2027 clock change on Halloween morning). It is citable because no ranking storefront compares types neutrally or cites the late-gift and voice-vs-text research, but two checklist items stay failed: there is no Halloween usage data behind any table column, and three of five sources (the EU clock rule and two general communication papers) could sit in a sibling post, with only the 159-card Neophilology study being about ecards at all, and that one is Russia Day cards read from the abstract. The fix pass also narrowed four unmeasured 'most' claims and two competitor-feature assertions, so the body now claims less than the draft did.

structuralLimitations: Fix pass 2026-10-22: removed unmeasured generalisations. 'What people send has drifted toward pictures' (Savelyeva shows dominance in one 159-card sample, not a trend) and 'in most ecards the words are the scarce part' were narrowed; 'Most Halloween ecards fall into one of four types' became a sorting statement; 'Most people also build close to the day' (sourced only to 89 SubhSandesh Raksha Bandhan pages) now names SubhSandesh creators.

Fix pass 2026-10-22: competitor-feature claims checked against the measured SERP. The ad-supported type asserted advertising on the card page, but 123cards was judged from its snippet only (HTTP 404), so the claim is now conditional ('where a catalogue runs on advertising'). The membership type said you add only a name and typed message, but americangreetings exposes an add-a-photo filter, so photos on designs that allow them are now mentioned. FAQ 'library ecards usually open from an email link' became 'also arrive as a link'.

The UK clock change on 31 Oct 2027 and the US dates (1 Nov 2026, 7 Nov 2027) are stated without a citation in this post; the EU directive does not bind the UK. Both were verified by sibling writers (b8 BRIEF §10; halloween-2027 cites gov.uk and NIST).
